1:
The month is identified before anything is said about the day. Gill names it Tisri, as the Targum of Jonathan has it, answering to part of our September and October, and famous for days to be religiously observed, having more of them than any other month. Clarke adds that this was the beginning of the civil year, a time of great festivity ushered in by trumpets. Henry gives reasons for the crowding: the month had been the first until the deliverance out of Egypt, which falling in Abib made that the beginning of the months in all ecclesiastical computations; it still stood first in the civil reckonings of jubilees and years of release; and it fell in the vacation between harvest and seedtime, when the people had most leisure for the sanctuary. From that he draws the lesson, that though God will dispense with sacrifices for works of necessity and mercy, the more leisure we have from this life’s pressing occasions the more we should spend in his immediate service.

What the day was for is answered two ways. Henry makes it preparatory, set before the two great solemnities that follow — holy mourning on the day of atonement and holy joy at tabernacles — and says the intention of divine institutions is answered when one service helps to fit us for another and all for heaven. Calvin looks at the passage rather than the day, observing that the festivals are not treated here but only the sacrifices that graced them; the day itself he calls the memorial of the blowing of trumpets. Henry adds a note on method: the trumpets had been appointed in Leviticus with no mention of these sacrifices, so that those who would know the mind of God must compare one part of scripture with another, the later discoveries explaining what was dark and supplying what was defective in the earlier.

The arithmetic of the offering draws the closest attention. Calvin notices that only one bullock is commanded, and explains it as befitting a minor festival; but the day was not therefore poorer, since two bullocks were already due on the first of every month, so that it carried three larger victims in all, the rest doubled to two rams and fourteen lambs. God consecrated the day doubly to himself, he concludes, so that one celebration diminished nothing of the other — the memorial of trumpets was not an abolition of the new moon, but both ordinances were kept at the same time. Henry turns it into a rule, that we must not seek occasions to abate our zeal nor be glad of an excuse to omit a good duty, since family worship does not excuse us from secret devotions. Clarke simply totals the day: one bullock, one ram, seven lambs, and a kid for a sin offering, besides the minchahs or meat offerings.

Two smaller points close the span. Gill explains that the meat offering went along with the creatures offered, the quantity of flour and oil for a bullock, a ram and each lamb being the same as at the new moons, unleavened bread and firstfruits; the kid was offered at this time as at those seasons and for the same purpose, to make atonement for the sins of their holy things. Clarke alone looks outside Israel, remarking that in imitation of the Jews different nations began their new year with sacrifices and festivity, that the ancient Egyptians did so, and that the Persians still celebrate their nawi rooz at the vernal equinox — the first day of the year being generally a time of festivity in all civilized nations.
6:
The first day’s offering is closed with a reminder of what it did not replace. Gill notes that the bullock, ram and seven lambs of this day were offered besides the two bullocks, one ram and seven lambs already due because it was the first day of the month, and besides the meat offering that went with them, none of which was omitted on account of the additions. Ellicott and Wesley agree on the phrase itself: Ellicott would render it the burnt offering of the new moon rather than of the month, pointing back to the description of the beginning of the month in the previous chapter, and Wesley glosses it as belonging to every new moon.

The tenth day is then introduced. Gill again names the month Tisri from the Targum of Jonathan; Ellicott sets the day in its legislation, that the law for its observance stands in Leviticus and that the sacrifices prescribed here — the same as those for the first day of the seventh month — were to be offered in addition to the sin offerings of atonement and to the daily burnt offerings. Calvin names it the day of Atonement and marks what distinguished it: although they never came into God’s presence without supplication for pardon, on this day they confessed their sins in a special manner, because a fast was appointed in token of their guilt, and Leviticus threatened that whatever soul was not afflicted that same day should be cut off from among his people.

What the affliction required is where the witnesses part. Wesley takes it plainly of fasting and abstinence from all delightful things, together with compunction for one’s sins and for the judgments of God either deserved or already inflicted. Ellicott agrees that the humiliation appears to have included fasting, and compares the reference in Acts, but immediately qualifies it: the word which denotes fasting is not employed here, nor is there any express injunction respecting fasting anywhere in the Pentateuch. Calvin does not raise the question, treating the fast as appointed and reading it as the token of guilt that the day required.

The sacrifices themselves are handled briefly and with one point of dispute. Calvin observes that one bullock only is required and the rest is as before, except that an exception is added which was omitted in the former cases: another propitiation is appointed besides the goat, to accord with the fact of their affliction — for the acknowledgment of guilt would have been a dreadful torment to their consciences without the hope of reconciliation. Gill takes the burnt offering to be the same as was ordered for the first day, but records that Aben Ezra held the ram here to be a different one; and he notes that the meat offering carried the same quantity of flour and oil for a bullock, a ram and a lamb as on the first day of the month. On the kid he adds a rule of order from the Jewish writers: because this goat differed from the one offered for the service of the day, it was offered after it, since a goat of the Musaphim, or additions, could not go before the service of the day itself.
12:
The feast is placed and then weighed. Gill dates it to the fifteenth of Tisri, the seventh month from Abib though once the first of the year. Calvin calls it the chief of their festivals and marks what separates it from the Passover: there they commemorated the night in which they came forth free from Egypt, whereas by dwelling in tabernacles seven days they embraced the whole forty years in which their fathers experienced God’s constant and consummate bounty, the assembly serving also for thanksgiving for the ingathering of the harvest. Ellicott gives that same second reason for the size of the offering, gratitude for the divine presence and protection and for the rich fruits recently gathered in. Wesley says what keeping seven days meant: not abstaining so long from all servile work, but offering extraordinary sacrifices each day. Henry makes the conjunction a principle, that their days of rejoicing were to be days of sacrifice, cheerfulness doing no harm when it enlarges our hearts in God’s service.

The tally is agreed and the reason for it is not. Clarke, Ellicott and Calvin count the same descending series — thirteen bullocks on the first day, twelve on the second, down to seven on the seventh, seventy in all — with two rams and fourteen lambs daily and a goat for a sin offering. Henry adds that the eighth day, though the great day of the feast, carried only one bullock, one ram and seven lambs. On why the number falls the witnesses divide widely. Henry answers first that the will of the Law-maker is reason enough; then reports the suggestion that God considered a flesh apt to grudge the expense of religion, ordering it to grow less lest they complain that he had made them to serve with an offering; then offers a third reading, that it intimates the legal dispensation waxing old, the many sacrifices ending in one great sacrifice infinitely more worthy — and he notes that it was on the last day of the feast, after all these had been ordered, that Christ cried to those still thirsting after righteousness to come to him and drink.

Calvin will not choose: why the distribution was so unequal is not clear to him, and he holds it better to confess ignorance than to vanish into mere smoke by too subtle speculation. He allows force to Scott’s conjecture, that the decrease until only one was offered on the last day may intimate the Mosaic institution waxing old and vanishing when the promised Messiah came. He then sets down an older opinion from De Lyra without endorsing it: the Hebrews say the offerings were made for other nations, seventy calves for seventy nations and languages, the daily decrease designating the dominion of the Gentiles terminated under King Messiah. That notion he calls neither curious nor to be rejected. What he will affirm is the arithmetic: diminishing daily they arrived on the seventh at seven, the symbol of perfection, the eighth superadded merely as a conclusion — where Ellicott independently calls seven the perfect number.

Two matters close the span. On the length of the recital Calvin holds Moses not careless, but securing that nothing be done except at God’s command and nothing altered by man’s fancy; Henry reaches the same end by another road, that the several appointment of each day is no vain repetition but a lesson in exactness, services repeated with an upright heart being no weariness to God. Henry adds that a sin offering was required daily, and that the continual burnt offering still stood first and last each day. Clarke alone counts the national cost: fifteen goats, twenty-one kids, seventy-two rams, a hundred and thirty-two bullocks and eleven hundred and one lambs a year, and even that little beside the passover lambs the priests counted for Cestius, who asked how many had come up to Jerusalem.
34:
What the eighth day is gets three different answers. Gill treats it as an appendix: it fell the day after the seven days of the feast of tabernacles were ended, and was not properly a part of that feast but a sort of appendage to it. Clarke reports the opposite valuation, that among the Jews this was esteemed the chief or high day of the feast, though fewer sacrifices were offered on it than on the others — the people seeming to have finished the solemnity with a greater measure of spiritual devotion; and he notes that it was on this day that Christ called the Jews from the letter to the spirit of the law, proposing himself as the sole fountain from which they could derive the streams of salvation. Ellicott would settle it by the word, rendering the phrase closing feast day rather than solemn assembly.

That rendering rests on a survey of the term. Ellicott observes that azereth, translated solemn assembly here and in the parallel passage in Leviticus, is used in Deuteronomy of the seventh or closing day of the Feast of the Passover, but that its other uses will not be confined to a last day: in Jeremiah it stands for an assembly or confederacy of false dealers, and in Amos it appears to include solemn festivals generally, without limitation to the last day of their duration. From that spread of usage he concludes that the primary notion is not assembly but restraint — from the performance of servile work.

On the offering itself the witnesses converge. Ellicott notes that the sacrifices of the eighth day were the same as those appointed for the first day of the seventh month, the Feast of Trumpets, and also for the tenth day, the Day of Atonement. Gill says the same from his own reckoning, that the burnt offering was that which had been offered on the first and tenth days of this month, with the meat and drink offerings for each of the creatures the same as have been often expressed; and he adds that on this day a goat for a sin offering was offered as well, besides the daily sacrifice and what went along with it.
39:
The chapter’s closing formula is challenged in the English before anything else is said about it. Gill objects to “in your set feasts” and would read rather “in the times set and appointed to you,” as the Jewish writers interpret it; he cites Jarchi, who takes it of a fixed time, and judges that reading the better one for a plain reason — these were not all feast days on which the above sacrifices were to be offered, since one of them was a fast, the day of atonement. Ellicott arrives at the same correction from the other side, preferring “These sacrifices shall ye offer unto the Lord at your set seasons.”

The second clause is read as a boundary. Ellicott takes the whole chapter’s prescriptions to have been appointed independently of all the burnt offerings, meal offerings, drink offerings and peace offerings which were made in performance of special vows or as freewill offerings, and refers the reader to the regulations in Leviticus and in the fifteenth chapter of Numbers, where vowed and freewill burnt offerings and peace offerings are prescribed. What the congregation owed, on this reading, neither absorbed nor excused what an individual might bring of his own accord.

The last verse divides the witnesses over where it belongs. Keil holds that it forms the conclusion of the list of sacrifices running through chapters twenty-eight and twenty-nine, so that the notice of Moses telling the people closes what has gone before. Ellicott records that in the Hebrew Bible this verse forms the beginning of the thirtieth chapter, which makes the same sentence an introduction rather than a conclusion. Neither offers an argument against the other, and the difference is left standing in the text itself. Gill reads the verse for its substance instead of its position: Moses told the children of Israel all these things, repeating the several laws to them concerning the sacrifices, with the additions made to them and the explanations of them, and did so according to all that the Lord commanded him, being a faithful servant to the Lord in all his house and in all things appertaining to it.
